rationale: A randomized Parkinson trial of 100 mg whole saffron powder tablets reported a 4.58-point depression improvement versus placebo. The separate Tehran trial favored saffron on Hamilton scores and had inconclusive secondary measures. A new selected non-Parkinson cohort had a smaller favorable result after standardized extract, while linked Shiraz comparisons remain inconclusive. The two Parkinson trials carry the lean against worsening and leave ordinary culinary exposure uncertain.

Two small dried rosemary capsule trials outside Parkinson disease reported lower depression scores. A newer heterogeneous synthesis is inconclusive for pooled depression. Fresh-derived beverage studies omitted clinical depression, a dementia odor comparison is inconclusive, and massage and inhalation results use different routes. The minimal lean against worsening rests on the dried oral trials.

A Parkinson Sargol powder trial favored overall sleep quality without a separate insomnia-severity result. Extract trials in other populations vary. One recent Affron study reports inconclusive PROMIS sleep disturbance and a favorable result on sleep-related impairment. The endpoint and formulation differences limit the lean toward benefit.

The randomized Isfahan report gives fatigue scores 9.20 points lower with saffron powder than placebo. Its standalone fatigue scale first appears in a public revision after manuscript receipt. A perimenopausal extract preprint reports lower fatigue on a different scale, and another non-Parkinson extract trial is inconclusive. The limited Parkinson evidence gives a weak lean against worsening.

Parkinson cohorts used cinnamon as a diagnostic odor. A five-odor program including cinnamon improved a composite smell score after infection. Ground cinnamon in an oral diabetes study gave an inconclusive meal-smell contrast and the mixed oil registration has no posted smell results. The clinical effect of eating ground cinnamon on Parkinson olfactory dysfunction remains unresolved.
